The Acts of the Apostles

Wheel of Heaven Translation

Four canon-cited Acts chapters: Acts 2 (Pentecost), 12 (Peter's prison release), 15 (Jerusalem Council), 17 (Areopagus)

Direct Direct Established or uncontested across mainstream sources, or a direct description of the project itself. Framework Framework Foundational premise of the Wheel of Heaven framework. Explicit in the Raëlian canon; not endorsed by mainstream scholarship. Inferred Inferred A reasonable reading of comparative material — not stated literally, but consistent with the source. Speculative Speculative Interpretive synthesis or hypothesis that goes beyond what any single source states.

Four canon-cited Acts chapters from the earliest substantial Koine Greek manuscript witnesses (Codex Vaticanus + Codex Sinaiticus + P45 Chester Beatty I ~250 CE for Acts; + NA28/UBS5/SBLGNT critical apparatus). Acts 2 (Pentecost), 12 (Peter prison release), 15 (Jerusalem Council Gentile-inclusion), 17 (Paul at the Areopagus + the Aratus citation). The Raëlian canon engages each of these chapters in *Extraterrestrials Took Me To Their Planet* — acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework applied at each canon-citation site per the established convention.

Chapter 2

Acts 2 — Pentecost: the tongues of fire descending + Peter's sermon citing Joel 2 the cosmic-signs

1
And when the day of Pentecost had fully come, they were all together in one place.
The former treatise I made, O Theophilus, concerning all that Jesus began both to do and to teach,
Καὶ Kai ἐν en τῷ tō συμπληροῦσθαι symplērousthai τὴν tēn ἡμέραν hēmeran τῆς tēs πεντηκοστῆς pentēkostēs ἦσαν ēsan πάντες pantes ὁμοῦ homou ἐπὶ epi τὸ to αὐτό. auto.
Notes Verse 1

The Pentecost opening at vv.1-4 integrates the Sinai-theophany imagery (Ex 19:16-19 thunder + cloud + shofar + fire) with the Num 11:24-30 Mosaic-spirit-distribution pattern. Pentecost (Greek pentēkostē) is the Greek name for the Jewish festival of Shavuot, the 50th day from Passover-Sabbath. In late-Second-Temple Judaism, Shavuot was associated both with the wheat-harvest first-fruits and with the Sinai-theophany / Torah-giving (rabbinic zĕman mattan tôrāṯēnū identification at Mekhilta Yitro 9; Jub 6:17-22). The Lukan choice of Pentecost as the spirit-outpouring timing is theologically-loaded: the event is framed as a Sinai-typological renewal. See central-glossary entry pentecost-acts-2-tongues-of-fire-sinai-num-11-cross-corpus.

Notes Verse 3

diamerizomenai glōssai hōsei pyros 'divided tongues as of fire'. The fire-and-tongue imagery integrates Sinai-theophany fire (Ex 19:18; 24:17 — the consuming fire on the mountain) with the rabbinic tradition (b. Šabbat 88b; Mekhilta Yitro) that at Sinai the divine-voice divided into 70 languages so all peoples could understand. The Acts 2:9-11 multinational audience-list at vv.9-11 functionally reactivates the Sinai-as-Torah-to-all-nations tradition.

Notes Verse 4

ērxanto lalein heterais glōssais 'they began to speak in other tongues'. The Lukan-Acts heterais glōssais ambiguity preserves both possible readings: xenoglossia (actual human-languages, supported by the vv.9-11 multinational audience list) vs glossolalia (ecstatic-spirit-language, as 1 Cor 12-14 develops). Both readings have textual warrant; the WoH-Translation does not adjudicate.

Notes Verse 9

The vv.9-11 multinational audience list (Parthians + Medes + Elamites + Mesopotamian-Judean-Cappadocian-Pontic-Asian + Phrygian-Pamphylian + Egyptian-Libyan + Roman + Cretan-Arabian) has been variously interpreted: an ecumenical-extent list, an astrological-zodiacal list (Hellenistic conventions), an order-following Jewish-diaspora-major-centers, or a tradition-bound list of the 70 nations of Gen 10. The Lukan-Acts framing is on the universal-extent of the apostolic mission. The 70-nations / Gen 10 background reinforces the Sinai-typological framing (the rabbinic tradition's 70-languages-at-Sinai).

Notes Verse 16

Peter's sermon centerpiece — the Joel 2:28-32 LXX (= MT Joel 3:1-5) citation at vv.17-21. The longest extended OT-citation in Acts and the explanatory framework for the Pentecost event. The citation deploys Joel as the explanatory-framework: the Spirit-outpouring inaugurates 'the last days', and the cosmic-signs are the eschatological-confirmation of the day-of-the-Lord context.

Peter substitutes en tais eschatais hēmerais 'in the last days' for Joel's meta tauta 'after these things' — a redactional adjustment that re-temporalizes Joel's prophecy as an inaugurated-eschatology statement. The substitution is one of the most-discussed Lukan-Acts editorial adjustments and is preserved in NA28/UBS5 critical text.

COSMIC-SIGNS CITATION (Joel 2:30-31 / 3:3-4 LXX). terata en tō ouranō anō kai sēmeia epi tēs gēs katō, haima kai pyr kai atmida kapnou 'wonders in the heaven above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and vapor of smoke'. Cross-corpus chain: Joel 2:30-31 → Mk 13:24-25 // Mt 24:29 → Lk 21:25-26 → Rev 6:12-13. The cosmic-signs cluster is one of the most-systematic NT redeployments of the Hebrew Bible prophetic-apocalyptic substrate. Documented at the central-glossary entry cosmic-signs-cluster-joel-2-mark-13-acts-2-luke-21-rev-6-cross-corpus. Bidirectional cross-corpus with v2.60.0 Qur'an inshiqaq-al-qamar-splitting-of-the-moon-sura-54-1.

Peter's kerygmatic sermon centerpiece engages two major HB citations — Ps 16:8-11 LXX (vv.25-28, the not-abandoned-to-Hades + not-seeing-corruption Davidic typology) and Ps 110:1 LXX (vv.34-35, the right-hand-of-the-Lord enthronement). Notes Verse 38

baptisthētō ... epi tō onomati Iēsou christou 'let each be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ'. The Acts-distinctive baptismal formula 'in the name of Jesus Christ' (cf. Acts 8:16; 10:48; 19:5) is structurally different from the Mt 28:19 triadic-formula 'in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit'. Modern scholarship widely accepts that the Acts formula reflects the earliest baptismal practice (cf. the Mt 28:19 Conybeare-hypothesis discussion at the existing central entry great-commission-mt-28-19-20-trinitarian-baptismal-formula-conybeare-hypothesis-cross-corpus-with-disavowals). The Acts pattern is documented as a structurally-distinct baptismal convention without theological-pre-resolution of the Trinitarian-vs-Christo-monotheistic dispute.

Notes Verse 6

MAJOR ANGELIC-DELIVERANCE NARRATIVE. Cross-corpus to Dan 3 (fiery-furnace-rescue) + Dan 6 (lion's-den-rescue) + Acts 5:17-26 (first apostolic prison-release). Characteristic features of the Lukan-Acts angelic-deliverance pattern: night-time setting + bright-light appearance + chains-falling-off + prison-gates opening of their own accord + iron-gate opening of its own accord. Documented at the central-glossary entry peter-prison-release-acts-12-daniel-6-angelic-deliverance-cross-corpus. The Raëlian-canon engagement (Raël 1975) is acknowledged-without-endorsement per the established framework.

Notes Verse 13

The Rhoda-narrative (vv.13-16) — Lukan-Acts narrative integrates humor into the deliverance-pattern: Rhoda hears Peter's voice at the gate but in her excitement leaves him knocking outside; the community doubts her ('You are out of your mind' v.15); they finally open the gate. The comic-narrative element distinguishes Acts 12 from the more-solemn Daniel-tradition.

Notes Verse 19

MAJOR APOSTOLIC-DECREE SITE. James' proposal (Acts 15:19-21) and the resulting decree-letter (15:23-29) establish the four-fold prohibition for Gentile-Christian membership: (i) idol-sacrifices; (ii) blood; (iii) strangled-things; (iv) porneia. Cross-corpus to Lev 17-18 (ger toshav / resident-alien commandments) and the rabbinic Noahide-commandments tradition. Documented at central-glossary entry apostolic-decree-acts-15-noahide-leviticus-17-18-cross-corpus. The Bauckham 1995 + Witherington 1998 + Bockmuehl 2000 monographs document the Lev 17-18 ger toshav background hypothesis.

Notes Verse 20

The four prohibitions: alisgēmatōn tōn eidōlōn / porneias / pniktou / haimatos — pollutions-of-idols + porneia + strangled-things + blood. The v.20 ordering (idol-pollutions + porneia + strangled-things + blood) differs from the v.29 ordering (idol-sacrifices + blood + strangled-things + porneia) — both preserved in the modern critical text. The four prohibitions are drawn from Lev 17-18 ger toshav commandments addressed to non-Israelite-residents.

Notes Verse 21

James' final rationale: Mōusēs gar ek geneōn archaiōn kata polin tous kēryssontas auton echei en tais synagōgais kata pan sabbaton anaginōskomenos 'For Moses from ancient generations has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath'. Two main interpretive lines: (i) the Sabbath-synagogue rationale (the prohibitions are chosen because they are familiar from the synagogue-Sabbath-Torah-reading); (ii) the Jewish-Christian-community rationale (the prohibitions enable table-fellowship between Jewish-Christians and Gentile-Christians in mixed congregations). Both readings have textual warrant.

Notes Verse 29

The decree-letter v.29 ordering: idol-sacrifices + blood + strangled-things + porneia. MAJOR TEXTUAL-CRITICAL LAYER. The Western text (Codex Bezae D/05) deploys a different reading: three-fold prohibition (idol-pollutions + blood + porneia) omitting 'strangled-things' AND adding the negative-Golden-Rule (kai hosa mē thelete heautois ginesthai heterō mē poiein 'and whatever you do not want done to yourselves, do not do to others'). The Western reading is widely interpreted as a 2nd-c. redaction emphasizing the moral over the dietary requirements after the Gentile-Christian-community had become demographically-dominant. The WoH-Translation preserves the Alexandrian critical-text four-fold prohibition per NA28/UBS5/SBLGNT.

TEXTUAL HOLE. v.34 is ABSENT in Vaticanus + Sinaiticus + Alexandrinus + P74 + the modern critical text. The verse is present in Bezae (D) and some Byzantine witnesses with the text edoxe de tō Sila epimeinai autou 'but it seemed good to Silas to remain there' — a Western interpolation smoothing the apparent narrative-inconsistency (v.33 says Judas and Silas were sent back to Antioch; v.40 has Paul taking Silas). The WoH-Translation preserves the modern critical-text convention: verse-number 34 is preserved as a 'hole'. See overlay-glossary entry acts-15-34-empty-verse-hole-western-interpolation-convention.

Notes Verse 22

MAJOR AREOPAGUS SPEECH — vv.22-31. Paul's natural-theology framework speech to the Athenian Areopagus court. The longest extended NT speech to a non-Jewish-non-Christian audience and the most-systematic Pauline engagement with Greek philosophical / poetic-tradition. Cross-corpus to Aratus Phaenomena line 5 (verbatim citation at v.28b) + Epimenides Cretica (citation at v.28a) + Stoic-Cleanthean Hymn to Zeus. Documented at central-glossary entry areopagus-speech-acts-17-22-31-natural-theology-aratus-epimenides-cross-corpus. The Raëlian-canon engagement is acknowledged-without-endorsement per the established framework.

Notes Verse 23

agnōstō theō 'to an unknown god'. Pausanias Description of Greece 1.1.4 reports altars to 'unknown gods' (theois agnōstois) on the road from Phaleron to Athens; Philostratus Vit. Apoll. 6.3.5 similarly attests Athenian altars 'even to unknown gods' (kai agnōstōn daimonōn). The plural altars are well-attested; the Lukan-Acts singular ('to AN unknown god') may be Lukan-redactional or may reflect a specific altar Paul encountered. Diogenes Laertius Lives 1.110 reports that Epimenides advised the Athenians to sacrifice 'to the appropriate god' without specifying which god, to avert a plague — the historical-religious-context for the unknown-god altar tradition.

MAJOR PHILOSOPHICAL-LITERARY CITATION SITE. Two verbatim Greek-tradition citations in one verse: (i) en autō gar zōmen kai kinoumetha kai esmen 'for in him we live and move and have our being' (v.28a) — widely attributed to a Cretica of Epimenides (6th-c. BCE Cretan philosopher-prophet), preserved in Syriac quotation in Isho'dad of Merv c. 850 CE; same source cited at Titus 1:12 (the Cretans-are-always-liars verse); (ii) tou gar kai genos esmen 'for we are also his offspring' (v.28b) — verbatim from Aratus Phaenomena line 5 (3rd-c. BCE Stoic-astronomical-poem opening hymn to Zeus). Aratus was Cilician (from Soli, near Tarsus) — a compatriot of Paul. The Stoic Cleanthes Hymn to Zeus offers a parallel Stoic-framing. Documented at central-glossary entry areopagus-speech-acts-17-22-31-natural-theology-aratus-epimenides-cross-corpus and overlay-glossary entry acts-17-28-aratus-quote-attribution-convention.

Being therefore the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man.
And now, Lord, look upon their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants to speak thy word with all boldness,
γένος genos οὖν oun ὑπάρχοντες hyparchontes τοῦ tou θεοῦ theou οὐκ ouk ὀφείλομεν opheilomen νομίζειν nomizein χρυσῷ chrysō ἢ ē ἀργύρῳ argyrō ἢ ē λίθῳ, lithō, χαράγματι charagmati τέχνης technēs καὶ kai ἐνθυμήσεως enthymēseōs ἀνθρώπου, anthrōpou, τὸ to θεῖον theion εἶναι einai ὅμοιον. homoion.
30
The times of ignorance, then, God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,
while thy stretchest forth thy hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of thy holy Servant Jesus.
τοὺς tous μὲν men οὖν oun χρόνους chronous τῆς tēs ἀγνοίας agnoias ὑπεριδὼν hyperidōn ὁ ho θεὸς theos τὰ ta νῦν nyn παραγγέλλει parangellei τοῖς tois ἀνθρώποις anthrōpois πάντας pantas πανταχοῦ pantachou μετανοεῖν, metanoein,
Notes Verse 30

The Christian-kerygmatic closing (vv.30-31): the call to universal repentance + the future-resurrection-judgment proclamation. The closing transitions from natural-theology to Christian-kerygma. The closing is rejected by part of the Areopagus audience (v.32 the resurrection mention provokes mockery) but accepted by some — including Dionysius the Areopagite and Damaris (v.34).

31
because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead."
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken wherein they were gathered together; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
καθότι kathoti ἔστησεν estēsen ἡμέραν hēmeran ἐν en ᾗ hē μέλλει mellei κρίνειν krinein τὴν tēn οἰκουμένην oikoumenēn ἐν en δικαιοσύνῃ dikaiosynē ἐν en ἀνδρὶ andri ᾧ hō ὥρισεν, hōrisen, πίστιν pistin παρασχὼν paraschōn πᾶσιν pasin ἀναστήσας anastēsas αὐτὸν auton ἐκ ek νεκρῶν. nekrōn.
32
Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said: "We will hear you again about this."
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and soul: and not one [of them] said that aught of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
ἀκούσαντες akousantes δὲ de ἀνάστασιν anastasin νεκρῶν nekrōn οἱ hoi μὲν men ἐχλεύαζον echleuazon οἱ hoi δὲ de εἶπαν· eipan· Ἀκουσόμεθά Akousometha σου sou περὶ peri τούτου toutou καὶ kai πάλιν. palin.
33
So Paul went out from their midst.
And with great power gave the apostles their witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus: and great grace was upon them all.
οὕτως houtōs ὁ ho Παῦλος Paulos ἐξῆλθεν exēlthen ἐκ ek μέσου mesou αὐτῶν. autōn.
34
But some men joined him and believed, among whom were Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
For neither was there among them any that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,
τινὲς tines δὲ de ἄνδρες andres κολληθέντες kollēthentes αὐτῷ autō ἐπίστευσαν, episteusan, ἐν en οἷς hois καὶ kai Διονύσιος Dionysios ὁ ho Ἀρεοπαγίτης Areopagitēs καὶ kai γυνὴ gynē ὀνόματι onomati Δάμαρις Damaris καὶ kai ἕτεροι heteroi σὺν syn αὐτοῖς. autois.
Notes Verse 34

Athenian converts (v.34): Dionysius the Areopagite — a member of the Areopagus court — is the most-prominent named convert. Later Christian tradition (the corpus pseudo-Dionysiacum, c. 500 CE) attributed a major mystical-theological corpus to this Dionysius, though the corpus is now widely-recognized as a 5th-6th-c. composition by an unknown author writing under the Dionysian pseudonym.

Contents

    Wheel of Heaven is an open, multilingual reading of the ancient world's creation traditions — Raëlian, biblical, Mesopotamian, and others — through a single working hypothesis: that the beings called Elohim were a small advanced human civilization that came here, designed life on Earth, and left a record in the religious texts. The reading runs across twelve ages of the precessional cycle, from the project's beginning twenty-two thousand years ago to the present age of disclosure and into the long future the next Great Year is opening. The site is free, source-aware, and built so the work can be checked.
